rendered:
The two papers use different methods to recover the PVDF binder:

The paper "Sustainable Direct Recycling of Lithium-Ion Batteries via Solvent Recovery of Electrode Materials" uses a thermally induced phase separation (TIPS) approach to recover the PVDF polymer. After reclaiming the active materials, the supernatant is composed of PVDF and CB in EG. By cooling down the hot supernatant to room temperature, phase separation occurs in which PVDF polymer precipitates out together with the residual CB particles.

The paper "Sustainable recycling of cathode scraps via Cyrene-based separation" uses a thermally induced phase separation (TIPS) approach as well. After reclaiming the active materials, the supernatant is composed of PVDF and CB in Cyrene. By cooling down the hot supernatant to room temperature, phase separation occurs in which PVDF polymer precipitates out together with the residual CB particles.

In both papers, the recovered PVDF polymer can be potentially reused as electrode binder or processed as membrane for desalination and water treatment.

If the question assumes something the documents contradict, say so. If the documents do not hold the answer, say so.

expect: premise false: ethylene glycol does not dissolve PVDF (cssc-2020 p5.L71-73); only Cyrene does (susmat-2020)
